title: Computer - Storage and Memory Devices
subject: ICT
description: Comprehensive practice on why computers need storage, storage units from bit to terabyte, permanent storage devices (hard drives, SSDs, USB, MicroSD, cloud), the history of storage from floppy disks to cloud (with India's tech journey and e-waste), RAM and ROM, RAM's role in multitasking and performance, real-world storage problem-solving, and the chapter's brain/nutrition and browser-history connections.

questions.question: What does computer storage allow a computer to do?
options: Save files, run programs, and remember settings
questions.explanation: Storage is essential for saving your work, running programs, and remembering settings on a computer.

questions.question: Which everyday object does the chapter compare to a computer to explain organising and storing information?
questions.explanation: The chapter opens by comparing bookshelves and computers, since both help organise and store information.

questions.question: Computers store information to help them perform tasks and run applications.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that computers store information so they can perform tasks and run applications.

questions.question: What are the two main types of computer storage described in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter divides computer storage into two types: Permanent Storage and Temporary Storage.

questions.question: Why does the chapter compare permanent storage to 'a digital filing cabinet'?
options: Because it keeps everything you create safely stored for later use, like paper files in a cabinet
Because it only stores digital photographs, nothing else
Because it works only when connected to the internet
Because it automatically deletes old files every day
questions.explanation: Permanent storage is described as being like a digital filing cabinet because it safely keeps everything you create for future use, just as a filing cabinet keeps paper documents.

questions.question: Temporary storage helps with which of these tasks?
options: Quick tasks like browsing and editing documents
questions.explanation: Temporary storage helps with quick tasks, like browsing the web and editing documents, while the computer is on.

questions.question: Temporary storage keeps files safe permanently, even after the computer is turned off.
questions.explanation: That is the job of permanent storage. Temporary storage is cleared when the computer is turned off.

questions.question: What happens to information in temporary storage when the computer is turned off?
options: It is moved to the cloud automatically
questions.explanation: Temporary storage is cleared when the computer is switched off, unlike permanent storage.

questions.question: The chapter compares temporary storage to remembering a phone number. What point is this example making?
options: Temporary storage holds information only until it is used once, like a phone number you dial and then forget
Temporary storage keeps information forever, like a saved contact
Temporary storage is only used for phone calls
Temporary storage is slower than permanent storage
questions.explanation: The phone-number example shows that temporary storage is used briefly for a task and then the information is not kept, just like remembering a number only long enough to dial it.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of using storage to save your work, according to the chapter?
options: Saving your password so you can log in faster
questions.explanation: The chapter gives the example that saving your password helps you log in faster next time.

questions.question: What happens when a computer's storage runs out, according to the chapter?
options: New files can't be saved, and the computer slows down
ROM automatically takes over all functions
questions.explanation: When storage runs out, new files can't be saved and the computer starts to slow down.

questions.question: Which of these statements about a computer with very little free storage space is FALSE?
options: It may not be able to save new files
It may not be able to install updates, risking security issues
It will always run faster because there is less clutter
questions.explanation: Having little free storage does not make a computer faster - it can prevent saving new files, slow the computer down, and even block updates, which is a security risk.

questions.question: Why can lack of storage space create security issues, according to the chapter?
options: Because it can prevent important software updates from installing
Because it makes the screen dimmer
Because it turns off the internet connection
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that a lack of storage can prevent updates, which can leave a computer with unpatched security issues.

questions.question: What appears on a computer screen when it is low on storage (memory)?
options: A warning message, like 'Your computer is low on memory'
An automatic shutdown with no warning
A request to change the wallpaper
questions.explanation: The chapter describes a warning message such as 'Your computer is low on memory' that appears when storage is low.

questions.question: Seeing a 'low on memory' warning message is a signal that you should free up storage space.
questions.explanation: The low-memory warning helps you know when to free up space on your computer.

questions.question: How does the chapter compare computers and human brains?
questions.explanation: The chapter draws a comparison between computers and human brains, since both store and process information.

questions.question: According to the chapter's opening question, what must we decide when storage space is limited?
options: What to keep and what to discard
What color to paint the computer
questions.explanation: The chapter's opening question asks what choices we must make when space and capacity are limited, meaning deciding what to keep and what to discard.

questions.question: Select ALL the things computer storage is needed for, according to the chapter.
questions.explanation: Storage is needed to save files, run applications, and remember settings. Screen brightness is unrelated to storage.

questions.question: A computer needs a certain amount of free storage space to operate...
questions.explanation: The chapter states that computers need a certain amount of free space to operate efficiently.

questions.question: Storage on a computer is only needed for saving photos and is never needed for running programs.
questions.explanation: Storage is needed for many things, including running applications and remembering settings, not just saving photos.

questions.question: Which description best matches 'Permanent Storage,' as given in the worksheet's fill-in-the-blank exercise?
options: It is like a digital filing cabinet where your computer stores everything you create
It is cleared the moment the computer is turned off
It is only used while actively browsing
It disappears after ten minutes of use
questions.explanation: The worksheet describes Permanent Storage as being like a digital filing cabinet that keeps everything you create.

questions.question: A student says, 'My computer doesn't need free storage space as long as it has electricity.' Why is this incorrect?
options: Because a computer needs a certain amount of free storage space to operate efficiently, regardless of power
Because electricity is actually a type of storage
Because computers never need storage space at all
Because storage space only matters when the computer is off
questions.explanation: Having electricity is not enough - the chapter explains that computers need free storage space to run efficiently, save files, and install updates.

questions.question: What do bookshelves and computers have in common, according to the chapter's introduction?
options: Both help organise and store information
questions.explanation: The chapter's introduction says that bookshelves and computers both help in organising and storing information.

questions.question: Which best explains why saving a password helps you 'log in faster,' as the chapter states?
options: Because it is stored so the computer doesn't need you to re-enter it every time
Because saved passwords make the internet faster
Because saving a password erases the need for a username
Because saved passwords are automatically shared with other computers
questions.explanation: When a password is saved in storage, the computer can recall it automatically instead of you retyping it, helping you log in faster.

questions.question: What is the smallest unit of computer storage?
questions.explanation: A bit is the smallest unit of computer storage.

questions.question: How many bits make up one byte?
questions.explanation: The chapter's storage-unit diagram shows that a byte is made up of 8 bits.

questions.question: What can a single byte typically store?
options: One letter, number, or special character
questions.explanation: A byte can store one letter, number, or special character.

questions.question: Put these storage units in the correct order, from smallest to largest.
options: Bit, Byte, Kilobyte, Megabyte, Gigabyte, Terabyte
Byte, Bit, Kilobyte, Megabyte, Gigabyte, Terabyte
Bit, Byte, Megabyte, Kilobyte, Gigabyte, Terabyte
Bit, Byte, Kilobyte, Gigabyte, Megabyte, Terabyte
questions.explanation: The correct order from smallest to largest is Bit, Byte, Kilobyte, Megabyte, Gigabyte, Terabyte. The other options swap the order of some units.

questions.question: What can a kilobyte (KB) typically store?
options: A short story or a few pictures
A small book or many pictures
questions.explanation: A kilobyte can store a short story or a few pictures, such as a digital photo.

questions.question: What can a megabyte (MB) typically store?
options: A small book or many pictures
A short story or a few pictures
Millions of books or a huge collection of movies
questions.explanation: A megabyte can store a small book or many pictures; a song might be a few megabytes.

questions.question: What can a gigabyte (GB) typically store, according to the worksheet's matching exercise?
options: A short story or a few pictures
A small book or many pictures
questions.explanation: A gigabyte can store multiple books, music, or videos - the chapter also gives the example that a movie might be a few gigabytes.

questions.question: What can a terabyte (TB) typically store?
options: Millions of books or a huge collection of movies
A short story or a few pictures
A small book or many pictures
questions.explanation: A terabyte can store millions of books or a huge collection of movies, and is often used for large data backups.

questions.question: How many bytes make up one kilobyte, according to the chapter's storage diagram?
questions.explanation: The chapter's block diagram shows that a Kilobyte (KB) is 1024 Bytes.

questions.question: How many kilobytes make up one megabyte?
questions.explanation: The chapter's block diagram shows that a Megabyte (MB) is 1024 KB.

questions.question: How many megabytes make up one gigabyte?
questions.explanation: The chapter's block diagram shows that a Gigabyte (GB) is 1024 MB.

questions.question: How many gigabytes make up one terabyte?
questions.explanation: The chapter's block diagram shows that a Terabyte (TB) is 1024 GB.

questions.question: According to the chapter's memory-trick mnemonic, what comes right after 'Kilobyte' in the sequence of storage units?
questions.explanation: The mnemonic 'Big Ben Knows to Make Good Tasty Porridge' places Megabyte right after Kilobyte (Bit, Byte, Kilobyte, Megabyte...).

questions.question: The chapter's memory trick is 'Big Ben Knows to Make Good Tasty Porridge.' What does the word 'Porridge' stand for in this sequence?
questions.explanation: In the mnemonic, 'Tasty' stands for Terabyte and 'Porridge' stands for Petabyte, the unit that comes right after Terabyte - it's easy to mix up these last two.

questions.question: A byte can store one letter, number, or special character.
questions.explanation: A byte is defined in the worksheet as being able to store one letter, number, or special character.

questions.question: A kilobyte is smaller than a byte.
questions.explanation: A kilobyte is much larger than a byte - one kilobyte equals 1024 bytes.

questions.question: According to the chapter's diagram, which pair correctly shows how Bit and Byte are denoted?
options: Bit is denoted 'b' (lowercase) and Byte is denoted 'B' (uppercase)
Bit is denoted 'B' (uppercase) and Byte is denoted 'b' (lowercase)
Both Bit and Byte are denoted with the same uppercase letter
Bit and Byte have no denoting letters at all
questions.explanation: The chapter's diagram shows a Bit is denoted by the letter 'b' and a Byte is denoted by 'B' - it is easy to mix up the upper and lower case.

questions.question: According to the 'Trail Treasure' fact, a nibble equals how many bits?
questions.explanation: The 'Trail Treasure' box states that a nibble is equal to 4 bits.

questions.question: In the early days of computing (the 1970s), computers could typically work with how many bits of data at a time?
questions.explanation: According to the 'Trail Treasure' history note, 1970s computers could only work with small amounts of data, like 4 bits (a nibble) at a time - later decades moved to 8-bit, then 16-bit and beyond.

questions.question: By the 1980s, according to the chapter's history note, which bit sizes could computers handle?
questions.explanation: The chapter states that by the 1980s, computers got better and could handle 8 bits and then 16 bits.

questions.question: Which bit sizes are described as common in modern computers, per the chapter's history note?
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that later, 32-bit and 64-bit computers became normal, making them much faster and more powerful.

questions.question: According to the worksheet's matching exercise, which storage unit matches 'a short story or a few pictures'?
questions.explanation: The worksheet's answer key matches Kilobyte to 'a short story or a few pictures.'

questions.question: According to the worksheet's matching exercise, which storage unit matches 'multiple books, music, or videos'?
questions.explanation: The worksheet's answer key matches Gigabyte to 'multiple books, music, or videos.'

questions.question: Select ALL storage units that are LARGER than a Megabyte.
questions.explanation: A Gigabyte and a Terabyte are both larger than a Megabyte. A Kilobyte and a Byte are both smaller than a Megabyte.

questions.question: A digital photo can typically be stored in which unit, according to the chapter's example?
questions.explanation: The chapter gives the example that a digital photo can be stored in kilobytes.

questions.question: A single song is typically a few of which unit, according to the chapter's fun fact?
questions.explanation: The chapter's fun fact says a song might be a few megabytes.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of permanent storage, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: Examples of permanent storage given in the chapter include hard drives and cloud storage.

questions.question: What is a key feature of permanent storage?
options: It keeps information safe even when the power is off
It loses everything the moment the power is off
It only works with an internet connection
It can only store text, never pictures
questions.explanation: Permanent storage keeps information safe even when the computer's power is off.

questions.question: The chapter compares permanent storage to what everyday object?
options: A bookshelf that keeps your books safe
questions.explanation: Permanent storage is compared to a bookshelf, which keeps your books safe over time.

questions.question: Which device has a large storage capacity but is typically slower compared to SSDs?
questions.explanation: Hard drives have large capacity but are slower compared to SSDs.

questions.question: What are USB drives also commonly known as?
questions.explanation: USB drives are also known as pen drives and can fit in your pocket.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of USB drives, according to the chapter?
options: They are portable and used for transferring files
They only work with an internet connection
They are the fastest storage type that exists
questions.explanation: USB drives are portable and are used for transferring files between computers.

questions.question: MicroSD cards are typically used in which type of devices?
questions.explanation: MicroSD cards are smaller versions of SD cards used in compact devices.

questions.question: MicroSD cards are typically used in desktop computers.
questions.explanation: MicroSD cards are typically used in compact devices, like smartphones, not desktop computers.

questions.question: What allows cloud storage to be accessed?
options: Any device with an internet connection
Only devices with a USB port
questions.explanation: Cloud storage allows access to data from any device with an internet connection.

questions.question: Cloud storage can only be accessed when you have an internet connection.
questions.explanation: Since cloud storage keeps data online, you need an internet connection to access it.

questions.question: What is a distinctive feature of cloud storage capacity, according to the chapter?
options: It can be unlimited, depending on the service
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that cloud storage can be unlimited, depending on the service you use.

questions.question: What does SSD stand for?
questions.explanation: SSD stands for Solid-State Drive, a modern, faster storage device.

questions.question: According to the worksheet's matching exercise, which device 'plugs into a USB port' and is small and portable?
questions.explanation: The worksheet describes the USB Drive as a small, portable device that plugs into a USB port.

questions.question: Which storage device, per the worksheet, 'stores data online and can be accessed from any device'?
questions.explanation: The worksheet matches Cloud Storage to 'stores data online and can be accessed from any device.'

questions.question: Which storage device, per the worksheet, is 'a traditional storage device inside most computers'?
questions.explanation: The worksheet matches Hard Drive to 'a traditional storage device inside most computers.'

questions.question: Which storage device, per the worksheet, 'is a modern, faster storage device for quicker data access'?
questions.explanation: The worksheet matches SSD to 'a modern, faster storage device for quicker data access.'

questions.question: Which storage device, per the worksheet, 'is a portable version of a hard drive that connects via USB'?
questions.explanation: The worksheet matches External Hard Drive to 'a portable version of a hard drive that connects via USB.'

questions.question: Which of these storage devices has the LARGEST typical capacity, according to the worksheet?
questions.explanation: Among these options, the External Hard Drive has the largest typical storage capacity.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of physical storage devices (like USB drives) over cloud storage, according to the worksheet?
options: They can be accessed without an internet connection
They can be accessed from any device
questions.explanation: Physical storage devices can be used without internet access, which is their advantage over cloud storage. Automatic backups, any-device access, and unlimited capacity are cloud storage advantages instead.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT typically an advantage of cloud storage, according to the chapter?
options: Being able to grow with the service
questions.explanation: Working without an internet connection is an advantage of physical storage devices, not cloud storage - cloud storage needs an internet connection to be accessed.

questions.question: A USB drive is an example of permanent storage.
questions.explanation: USB drives keep data safely stored even when disconnected from power, making them permanent storage.

questions.question: Why might someone choose a hard drive over an SSD, despite it being slower?
options: Because hard drives typically offer larger storage capacity for the price
Because hard drives are always faster than SSDs
Because hard drives need no electrical power at all
Because hard drives are actually a type of RAM
questions.explanation: Hard drives are slower than SSDs but typically offer larger storage capacity, which is why they may still be chosen.

questions.question: Select ALL examples of permanent storage devices mentioned in the chapter.
questions.explanation: Hard drives, USB drives, and cloud storage are all permanent storage. RAM is temporary storage, not permanent.

questions.question: Which of these best describes 'permanent storage,' as summarised in the chapter's Quick Guide?
options: Your Digital Cupboard - keeps things safe even when the power is off
Your Digital Desk - keeps things only while you're working
Your Digital Camera - takes pictures only
Your Digital Speaker - plays music only
questions.explanation: The chapter's Quick Guide describes Permanent Storage as 'Your Digital Cupboard,' which keeps things safe even when the power is off.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: Which storage device was commonly used in the 1980s and 1990s?
questions.explanation: Floppy disks were an early form of data storage used in the 1980s and 1990s.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: About how much data could an early floppy disk store?
questions.explanation: An early floppy disk could store about 80 KB of data.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: How much data could a 3.5-inch floppy disk store?
questions.explanation: The chapter's interesting information notes that 3.5-inch floppy disks could store 1.44 MB.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: Which storage devices followed floppy disks, storing more data like music and movies?
questions.explanation: CDs and DVDs followed floppy disks, and could store more data such as music and movies.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: About how much music can a standard CD hold?
questions.explanation: A standard CD holds about 80 minutes of music.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: About how much data can a standard CD store?
questions.explanation: A standard CD holds about 700 MB of data.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: How much data can a DVD store, according to the chapter's fun fact?
questions.explanation: The chapter's fun fact says DVDs can store up to 4.7 GB of data.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: What is the correct historical order of storage evolution, according to the chapter?
options: Floppy disks, then CDs/DVDs, then USB drives, then Cloud storage
Cloud storage, then floppy disks, then CDs/DVDs, then USB drives
USB drives, then floppy disks, then Cloud storage, then CDs/DVDs
CDs/DVDs, then floppy disks, then Cloud storage, then USB drives
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that floppy disks led to CDs, then USB drives, and finally cloud storage - the other orders scramble this sequence.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: What did each advancement in storage technology allow, according to the chapter?
options: Using more electricity for the same result
questions.explanation: The chapter states that each advancement in storage technology allowed for more data to be stored.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: Floppy disks came before CDs and DVDs in the history of computer storage.
questions.explanation: Floppy disks were an earlier storage technology; CDs and DVDs followed them, storing even more data.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: How did India contribute to the history of technology and storage, according to the chapter?
options: Indian engineers helped maximise storage efficiency, reflected in today's tech leadership
India banned the use of cloud storage
India only uses old storage methods today
questions.explanation: The chapter states that Indian engineers maximised storage efficiency, which is reflected in today's tech leadership.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: According to the chapter's fun fact, India's tech journey moved from floppy disks to what?
questions.explanation: The chapter's fun fact says that from floppy disks to managing massive data centers, India's tech journey is inspiring.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: What environmental concern is linked to advances in storage technology, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that storage advancements have an environmental impact through e-waste.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: Which of these is given as an eco-friendly storage option in the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter gives energy-efficient SSDs as an example of an eco-friendly storage choice.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: How does recycling old storage devices help, according to the chapter?
options: It reduces waste and energy consumption
It increases the device's storage capacity
It automatically makes the device faster
It prevents any future data loss
questions.explanation: Recycling old devices helps reduce waste and energy consumption, according to the chapter.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: Which storage medium described in the chapter's history has the SMALLEST typical capacity?
questions.explanation: Of the capacities mentioned, an early floppy disk's roughly 80 KB is the smallest - even smaller than the improved 3.5-inch floppy disk's 1.44 MB.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: Select ALL storage technologies that came AFTER floppy disks, according to the chapter's history of storage.
questions.explanation: CDs, DVDs, and cloud storage all followed floppy disks in the chapter's timeline. Floppy disks themselves are the starting point, not something that came after.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: Which two optical disc formats does the chapter mention as following floppy disks?
questions.explanation: The chapter mentions CDs and DVDs as the storage formats that followed floppy disks.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: According to the chapter, choosing eco-friendly storage options can help reduce environmental impact.
questions.explanation: The chapter recommends eco-friendly options, like energy-efficient SSDs, to help reduce the environmental impact of storage technology.

questions.topic: History of Storage, India's Tech Journey and E-Waste
questions.question: Why does the chapter highlight the history of storage devices?
options: To show how storage technology has evolved over time, storing more and more data
To prove that floppy disks are still the best option today
To show that storage technology never changes
To argue that computers don't actually need storage
questions.explanation: The chapter's history section shows how storage technology evolved, with each new device able to store more data than the one before.

questions.question: What does RAM stand for?
questions.explanation: RAM stands for Random Access Memory.

questions.question: What does ROM stand for?
questions.explanation: ROM stands for Read Only Memory.

questions.question: Which type of memory is used for temporary tasks while the computer is on?
questions.explanation: RAM is used for temporary tasks while the computer is on.

questions.question: Which type of memory stores permanent instructions that do not change?
questions.explanation: ROM stores permanent instructions that do not change.

questions.question: The chapter compares RAM to a desk. What point is this comparison making?
options: RAM is used temporarily while working, like a desk holds things only while you use them
RAM never changes, like a permanent bookshelf
RAM is always empty and unused
RAM only works with an internet connection
questions.explanation: RAM is like a desk - you keep things on it only while you're working, and it's cleared once you're done, just as RAM is cleared when the computer is off.

questions.question: RAM is considered volatile memory because it loses data when the computer is turned off.
questions.explanation: RAM is volatile memory - it loses its data as soon as the computer is turned off.

questions.question: Why is ROM considered 'non-volatile'?
options: It retains data even when the computer is turned off
It loses data instantly when idle
It needs a constant internet connection
It only works while the computer is charging
questions.explanation: ROM is non-volatile, meaning it retains its data even when the computer is turned off.

questions.question: ROM loses its data when the computer is turned off.
questions.explanation: ROM does not lose its data when the computer is off - it is non-volatile and retains its information.

questions.question: What does ROM help the computer do every time it is turned on?
questions.explanation: ROM contains instructions to start the computer, helping it boot up correctly every time.

questions.question: RAM is essential for which of these tasks?
options: Starting up the computer for the very first time
questions.explanation: RAM is essential for running apps and games smoothly while the computer is on.

questions.question: What does more RAM allow a computer to do, according to the chapter?
options: Open multiple browser tabs without slowing down
questions.explanation: More RAM allows you to open multiple browser tabs without the computer slowing down.

questions.question: A computer with 8 GB RAM will generally run faster (for multitasking) than a computer with 2 GB RAM.
questions.explanation: More RAM generally allows a computer to handle multiple tasks more smoothly, so 8 GB RAM outperforms 2 GB RAM for multitasking.

questions.question: According to the chapter's comparison table, which is generally FASTER: RAM or ROM?
questions.explanation: The comparison table shows RAM is fast memory used when running programs, while ROM is slower but always available.

questions.question: RAM is typically larger in size compared to ROM.
questions.explanation: The comparison table shows RAM is usually larger in size compared to ROM.

questions.question: According to the chapter's 'Functions' comparison, what does RAM help a computer do?
options: Do tasks quickly, like opening apps or games
Store instructions for starting the computer
questions.explanation: The Functions row of the comparison table shows RAM helps the computer do tasks quickly, like opening apps or games.

questions.question: According to the chapter's 'Functions' comparison, what does ROM store?
options: Important instructions that help the computer start
questions.explanation: The Functions row of the comparison table shows ROM stores important instructions that help the computer start.

questions.question: According to the 'RAM vs ROM: The Simple Story' table, what is RAM's 'Job'?
questions.explanation: In the RAM vs ROM table, RAM's Job is described as 'Active helper.'

questions.question: According to the 'RAM vs ROM: The Simple Story' table, what is ROM's 'Job'?
questions.explanation: In the RAM vs ROM table, ROM's Job is described as 'Permanent guide.'

questions.question: In the 'RAM vs ROM' table's real-life example, RAM is compared to what?
questions.explanation: The table's real-life example compares RAM to 'your homework on the desk' - something actively being used.

questions.question: In the 'RAM vs ROM' table's real-life example, ROM is compared to what?
questions.explanation: The table's real-life example compares ROM to 'your textbook on the shelf' - something permanent and unchanging.

questions.question: According to the 'RAM vs ROM' table's 'Change' row, which best describes RAM?
questions.explanation: The 'Change' row of the table describes RAM as 'Changes constantly,' in contrast to ROM which is 'Fixed forever.'

questions.question: According to the 'RAM vs ROM' table's 'Change' row, which best describes ROM?
questions.explanation: The 'Change' row of the table describes ROM as 'Fixed forever,' in contrast to RAM which 'Changes constantly.'

questions.question: Which memory type is described as 'always available,' even though it is slower?
questions.explanation: The comparison table describes ROM as slower compared to RAM, but always available.

questions.question: A student says, 'Since ROM is slower, it must be worse than RAM.' Why is this misleading?
options: Because RAM and ROM serve different purposes - ROM's job is to reliably store permanent startup instructions, not to be fast
Because ROM is actually always faster than RAM
Because RAM is completely useless compared to ROM
Because RAM and ROM are exactly identical
questions.explanation: Speed isn't the right way to judge ROM, since its purpose is to reliably store permanent instructions the computer needs to start, not to be the fastest memory.

questions.question: RAM and ROM are both described as which type of memory in the chapter?
questions.explanation: Both RAM and ROM are called main memory, essential for computer functions.

questions.question: Bits are described in the chapter as which of the following?
options: The smallest unit of computer storage
The largest unit of computer storage
questions.explanation: Bits are the smallest unit of computer storage.

questions.question: Select ALL statements that are TRUE about RAM.
options: It is generally faster than ROM
It is used for active, running tasks
It retains data forever, even with the power off
questions.explanation: RAM is temporary/volatile, faster than ROM, and used for active tasks. It does NOT retain data with the power off - that is ROM's job.

questions.question: Select ALL statements that are TRUE about ROM.
options: It is generally slower than RAM
It loses its data when the power is off
questions.explanation: ROM is non-volatile, stores startup instructions, and is slower than RAM. It does NOT lose its data when the power is off - that is RAM's behaviour.

questions.question: A text message is stored using which unit, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter states that a text message is stored in bytes, since a byte can store letters and characters.

questions.question: Why can't a computer start up properly without ROM, according to the chapter?
options: Because ROM holds the essential instructions the computer needs to boot and connect its devices
Because ROM makes the screen brighter
Because ROM stores all of your personal photos
Because ROM automatically connects to Wi-Fi
questions.explanation: ROM houses essential instructions for computer operation, and ensures the computer starts correctly every time it is turned on.

questions.question: What is RAM crucial for, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: RAM is crucial for multitasking on a computer.

questions.question: What does more RAM allow, in terms of multitasking?
options: Smoother performance when using multiple applications
The computer to turn off faster
The computer to need less electricity
questions.explanation: More RAM allows for smoother performance when using multiple applications at once.

questions.question: According to the chapter's example, how much RAM can handle several applications at once without slowing down?
questions.explanation: The chapter's example states that 8 GB of RAM can handle several applications at once without slowing down.

questions.question: A student believes: 'If a computer has a lot of storage space, it will always work fast.' Why is this a misconception, according to the chapter's 'Detour' box?
options: Because speed depends more on RAM (like a study table) than on total storage space (like a bookshelf)
Because storage space has nothing at all to do with computers
Because RAM and storage space are the exact same thing
Because computers never slow down for any reason
questions.explanation: The Detour box explains that speed depends more on memory (RAM), which is like a study table, not on how much storage space (the bookshelf) a computer has.

questions.question: In the chapter's bookshelf-and-desk analogy about computer speed, what does the 'study table' represent?
questions.explanation: In the analogy, the study table represents RAM - the memory used for active work.

questions.question: In the chapter's bookshelf-and-desk analogy about computer speed, what does the 'bookshelf' represent?
options: Storage (where files and books are kept)
questions.explanation: In the analogy, the bookshelf represents storage, where files are kept long-term - separate from RAM, the study table used for active work.

questions.question: Even with a big 'bookshelf' (lots of storage), why might a computer still run slowly, according to the Detour box?
options: Because the 'study table' (RAM) is small and crowded
Because storage should never be kept full
Because the bookshelf is too well organised
Because there are simply too many files stored
questions.explanation: The Detour box explains that even with plenty of storage, if the study table (RAM) is small and crowded, work becomes slow.

questions.question: In the performance chart, what happens when opening just ONE browser tab with a simple game or video, regardless of whether the computer has 2 GB, 4 GB, or 8 GB of RAM?
options: The computer runs smoothly in all three cases
It only works with 8 GB RAM
questions.explanation: The performance chart shows that opening one tab with a simple game or video runs smoothly on 2 GB, 4 GB, and 8 GB of RAM alike.

questions.question: According to the performance chart, what happens with 2 GB RAM when opening two browser tabs, playing music, and using a word processor together?
options: The computer starts to slow down and take time to open things
questions.explanation: With only 2 GB of RAM, doing these tasks together causes the computer to slow down and take time to open things.

questions.question: According to the performance chart, what happens with 4 GB RAM for the same multitasking (two tabs, music, and a word processor)?
options: The computer can handle it easily, switching between tasks without waiting
questions.explanation: With 4 GB of RAM, the computer can handle these tasks easily and switch between them without waiting.

questions.question: According to the performance chart, what happens with only 2 GB RAM when opening several browser tabs, playing a game, AND using a photo editing program at the same time?
options: The computer may freeze or even crash
questions.explanation: With only 2 GB of RAM, this heavy combination of tasks may cause the computer to freeze or crash.

questions.question: Which RAM size, according to the performance chart, allows a computer to run quickly and juggle many heavy tasks (several tabs, a game, and a photo editor) at once?
questions.explanation: The performance chart shows that 8 GB of RAM runs quickly and juggles many tasks at once, even the heaviest combination.

questions.question: For someone who mainly uses a computer to watch a video or play a simple game, how much RAM does the worksheet suggest is sufficient?
questions.explanation: The worksheet's answer key states that 2 GB of RAM is sufficient for watching a video or playing a simple game.

questions.question: For someone who writes a story while listening to music and browsing the web, what minimum RAM does the worksheet recommend?
questions.explanation: The worksheet's answer key recommends a minimum of 4 GB RAM for writing a story while listening to music and browsing the web.

questions.question: Based on the performance chart, which RAM amount is the minimum needed to handle two tabs, music, and a word processor together WITHOUT slowing down?
questions.explanation: The chart shows that 2 GB slows down for this combination, but 4 GB (and 8 GB) can handle it easily - so 4 GB is the minimum needed to avoid slowdown.

questions.question: RAM is crucial for multitasking on a computer.
questions.explanation: The chapter directly states that RAM is crucial for multitasking on a computer.

questions.question: Which best summarises the relationship between RAM and multitasking, according to the chapter?
options: More RAM generally means smoother performance with multiple applications running at once
More RAM means less storage space overall
More RAM makes the screen physically bigger
RAM has no effect on multitasking at all
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that more RAM allows smoother performance when using multiple applications at once.

questions.question: Select ALL scenarios where a computer with only 2 GB of RAM might struggle or slow down, according to the performance chart.
options: Opening two tabs, music, and a word processor together
Opening several tabs, a game, and a photo editor together
Opening one tab with a simple game or video
questions.explanation: The performance chart shows 2 GB RAM slows down or may even crash with heavier multitasking, but runs smoothly with just one simple tab.

questions.question: What is the main lesson of the chapter's 'Golden Rule' about storage and memory?
options: Important files need permanent storage; quick tasks need temporary storage
Everything should always be stored in RAM
Nothing on a computer needs any storage at all
ROM should be used to store your photos
questions.explanation: The chapter's Golden Rule states that important files need permanent storage, while quick tasks need temporary storage.

questions.question: Why does the chapter say 'Storage is like a bookshelf... Speed depends more on memory (RAM)'?
options: To clarify that having lots of storage space doesn't guarantee a fast computer - RAM affects speed and multitasking more directly
To say that storage doesn't matter at all for computers
To say that RAM and storage are identical things
To say that computers never actually need RAM
questions.explanation: This comparison clarifies that storage space alone doesn't determine speed; RAM has a bigger direct effect on how quickly and smoothly a computer can multitask.

questions.question: How many videos does Samira need to store, according to the worksheet scenario?
questions.explanation: In the worksheet scenario, Samira has 5 videos to store, each 1 GB in size.

questions.question: How large is each of Samira's videos?
questions.explanation: Each of Samira's 5 videos is 1 GB in size.

questions.question: How many photos does Samira have to store?
questions.explanation: Samira has 200 photos to store, each 5 MB in size.

questions.question: How large is each of Samira's photos?
questions.explanation: Each of Samira's 200 photos is 5 MB in size.

questions.question: How many documents does Samira need to store?
questions.explanation: Samira has 10 documents to store, each 500 KB in size.

questions.question: How large is each of Samira's documents?
questions.explanation: Each of Samira's 10 documents is 500 KB in size.

questions.question: How large is Samira's one game file?
questions.explanation: Samira's one game file is 3 GB in size.

questions.question: According to the worksheet's answer key, what is the total storage Samira needs for all her items?
questions.explanation: The worksheet's answer key gives the total storage needed as 9.005 GB, or 9 GB and 5 MB.

questions.question: Does everything Samira wants to store fit on an 8 GB USB drive?
options: No, since her total need (about 9 GB) is more than 8 GB
Yes, but only if she deletes the game
Yes, but only the videos fit
questions.explanation: Since Samira needs about 9 GB in total, it does not all fit on an 8 GB USB drive - the answer key confirms 'No.'

questions.question: If Samira only has 5 GB of free cloud storage, which of her items could she store there entirely, per the answer key?
questions.explanation: The answer key suggests Samira could store her 5 videos (5 GB total) in the cloud, since this fits within her 5 GB of free cloud space.

questions.question: Besides storing all 5 videos in the cloud, what is another valid option the answer key gives for what to put in the cloud?
questions.explanation: The answer key also allows storing the 200 photos and 10 documents together in the cloud, since their combined size fits within 5 GB.

questions.question: According to the answer key, could Samira also choose to store just her 1 game (3 GB) in the cloud?
options: Yes, since 3 GB fits within her 5 GB of free cloud space
No, the game is too big for the cloud
No, games can never be stored in the cloud
Yes, but only using an SSD
questions.explanation: The answer key allows any combination adding up to between about 1.005 GB and 5 GB, so storing just the 3 GB game in the cloud is a valid option.

questions.question: Why can't Samira simply ignore the 8 GB limit and save all her files to the USB drive anyway?
options: Because a storage device can only hold as much data as its capacity allows; once full, no more files can be saved
Because USB drives automatically expand their capacity when needed
Because storage limits don't really apply to USB drives
Because the files would automatically shrink to fit
questions.explanation: A storage device's capacity is a real limit - once it is full, no more files can be saved, which is why Samira must plan which files go where.

questions.question: If Samira wants to reduce what she has to manage on her USB drive, which strategy best matches the answer key's suggestion?
options: Move large items (like the videos or the game) to the cloud, since together they use much of her free cloud space
Move only the smallest documents to the cloud
Delete all of her files immediately
Avoid using any additional storage at all
questions.explanation: The answer key's suggestions focus on moving larger items (like all 5 videos, or the game) to the cloud to make the best use of her limited free cloud space.

questions.question: Samira's total storage need (about 9 GB) is more than what her 8 GB USB drive can hold.
questions.explanation: Since Samira needs about 9 GB total and her USB drive holds only 8 GB, everything cannot fit on the USB drive alone.

questions.question: According to the answer key, Samira can store her 200 photos and 10 documents together in the cloud if she has 5 GB free.
questions.explanation: The 200 photos (1000 MB) plus 10 documents (5000 KB) together take up just over 1 GB, which comfortably fits within 5 GB of free cloud space.

questions.question: What real-world storage skill does Samira's problem help practice?
options: Deciding which files to prioritise when storage space is limited
questions.explanation: Samira's storage problem helps practice calculating storage needs and deciding which files to prioritise when space is limited.

questions.question: Which of Samira's item types takes up the LEAST total space, across all items of that type?
options: Her 10 documents (500 KB each, about 4.88 MB total)
questions.explanation: Samira's 10 documents at 500 KB each add up to only about 4.88 MB total, far less than her videos, photos, or game.

questions.question: Which of Samira's item types takes up the MOST total space, across all items of that type?
questions.explanation: Samira's 5 videos at 1 GB each total 5 GB, which is more than her game (3 GB), her photos (about 0.98 GB), or her documents (about 4.88 MB).

questions.question: If Samira had to choose ONE type of file to delete first to free up the most space, which should she pick?
options: Her videos (since they take up the most total space, 5 GB)
Her documents (since they take up the least total space)
questions.explanation: Since Samira's 5 videos together take up the most total space (5 GB), deleting them would free up the most space, though her documents take up the least space and would free the least.

questions.question: What kind of real-life skill does matching a storage device to its description (as in the worksheet) help build?
options: Recognising and choosing the right storage device for a situation
questions.explanation: Matching storage devices to their descriptions helps students recognise and choose the right storage device for different situations.

questions.question: According to the answer key, storing just the game (3 GB) in the cloud while keeping the videos, photos, and documents on the USB drive is one acceptable solution.
questions.explanation: If the 3 GB game goes to the cloud, the remaining videos, photos, and documents total under 6 GB, which fits comfortably on the 8 GB USB drive, and 3 GB fits within the 5 GB cloud limit.

questions.question: What does this worksheet activity mainly teach students to do?
options: Calculate total storage needs and make decisions about where to store different files
questions.explanation: The activity teaches students to calculate total storage needs and decide where to store different files given limited space.

questions.question: What is the title of the chapter's opening section that poses its guiding question?
questions.explanation: The chapter's opening section, which poses its guiding question, is titled 'Embark.'

questions.question: According to the chapter's opening ('Embark') question, what must we decide when space and capacity are limited?
options: What to keep and what to discard
questions.explanation: The Embark question asks what choices we must make about knowledge and storage when space and capacity are limited - namely, what to keep and what to discard.

questions.question: The chapter's opening image shows a computer alongside which other object, to represent organising and storing knowledge?
questions.explanation: The opening image pairs a computer with a bookshelf full of books, tying together how both organise and store knowledge.

questions.question: According to the 'Nutrition Junction' section, which foods are highlighted as rich in Omega-3 and good for memory?
questions.explanation: 'Nutrition Junction' highlights almonds and walnuts as rich in Omega-3, improving memory.

questions.question: How many almonds does the chapter suggest snacking on before computer class?
questions.explanation: The chapter suggests snacking on 5-6 almonds before computer class.

questions.question: According to 'Nutrition Junction,' which food provides quick energy for the brain, similar to how RAM needs energy to function?
questions.explanation: Bananas provide quick energy for the brain, which the chapter compares to how RAM needs energy to function.

questions.question: According to 'Nutrition Junction,' about what percentage of our bodies is water?
questions.explanation: The chapter states that our bodies are about 60% water.

questions.question: Why does the chapter compare water to 'the ultimate storage for your body'?
options: Because just as computers need memory, our bodies need hydration to function well
Because water is used to physically cool down computer chips
Because water can literally store computer files
Because water is described as a type of RAM
questions.explanation: The comparison highlights that just as computers need memory to function, our bodies need hydration (water) to function well.

questions.question: How often does the chapter suggest drinking water during computer work?
questions.explanation: The chapter suggests drinking water every 30 minutes during computer work.

questions.question: According to 'Nutrition Junction,' which food is good for your eyes and helps reduce strain while reading file sizes or organising folders?
questions.explanation: Carrots are described as good for the eyes, helping reduce strain when reading file sizes or organising folders on screen.

questions.question: In the 'Indian Thali Approach to Digital Learning,' what do proteins like dal or paneer help build?
questions.explanation: The chapter's thali analogy states that proteins (dal/paneer) build strong memory skills.

questions.question: In the 'Indian Thali Approach,' what do carbs like rice or roti give you?
questions.explanation: The thali analogy states that carbs (rice/roti) give energy for problem-solving.

questions.question: In the 'Indian Thali Approach,' what role do vegetables play?
questions.explanation: The thali analogy states that vegetables keep eyes and brain healthy.

questions.question: In the 'Indian Thali Approach,' what does curd help with?
questions.explanation: The thali analogy states that curd aids digestion and focus.

questions.question: What playful term does the chapter use for the human brain in the 'Nutrition Junction' section?
questions.explanation: The chapter playfully calls the human brain your 'biological RAM,' linking brain health to computer memory concepts.

questions.question: According to the chapter, what you eat can affect how well you use computers.
questions.explanation: 'Nutrition Junction' explains the connection between diet and how well you understand and use computers.

questions.question: What is the main message of the 'Nutrition Junction' section's closing 'Remember' note?
options: A well-nourished body supports a sharp mind, which learns computer concepts faster
Eating has no effect on learning at all
Only water matters for learning, not food
Food should be avoided before computer class
questions.explanation: The closing note says a well-nourished body supports a sharp mind, and a sharp mind learns computer concepts faster.

questions.question: What is the name of the chapter's activity page about researching storage companies and checking browser history?
questions.explanation: The activity about researching storage companies and checking browser history is titled 'Cyber Station.'

questions.question: In the 'Cyber Station' activity, after closing all windows and restarting the computer, what happens to the previously visited websites in the browser history?
options: They are still available/visible in the history
questions.explanation: The activity asks students to check that browser history remains visible even after a restart, showing that this data is not lost.

questions.question: Based on the 'Cyber Station' activity's finding that browser history survives a restart, is browser history part of permanent storage or temporary storage?
options: Permanent storage, since it is saved and available even after the computer restarts
Temporary storage, since browsing happens on the screen
Neither - browser history isn't stored at all
Both equally, with no real difference
questions.explanation: Since browser history remains available even after a shutdown and restart, it must be saved in permanent storage rather than being cleared like temporary storage.

questions.question: While you are actively browsing a webpage, which type of storage is being used to show the website content on screen at that moment?
options: Temporary storage (RAM), for quick access while the page is open
Permanent storage, since websites are saved forever
None - browsers don't use any storage
questions.explanation: While actively browsing, temporary storage (RAM) is used to quickly display the website content on screen, even though the browsing history itself gets saved permanently.

questions.question: What does the chapter's opening question suggest a bookshelf and a computer can both teach us about?
options: How humans collect, organise, protect, and value knowledge
How to fix a broken computer
How to build a wooden bookshelf
How to browse the internet faster
questions.explanation: The Embark question asks what a bookshelf and a computer can teach us about how humans collect, organise, protect, and value knowledge.

questions.question: According to the Cyber Station activity, checking your browser history after a restart proves that some browsing data is saved permanently, not just temporarily.
questions.explanation: Because the browser history remains after a restart, this shows it is saved in permanent storage rather than being cleared like temporary data.

questions.question: Which food from 'Nutrition Junction' is specifically linked to helping digestion and focus?
questions.explanation: Curd is linked in the chapter's thali analogy to aiding digestion and focus.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: What are microprocessor chips compared to, in the chapter?
questions.explanation: Microprocessor chips are described as being like tiny brains for computers.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: What do microprocessor chips help a computer do?
questions.explanation: Microprocessor chips help process tasks and run applications on a computer.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: What does a computer's speed mainly depend on, according to the chapter's microprocessor fact?
options: The number of USB ports it has
questions.explanation: The chapter states that a computer's speed depends on the microprocessor's efficiency.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: Which units help measure file sizes, according to the chapter?
questions.explanation: Bytes, kilobytes, and gigabytes help measure file sizes.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: Different types of files require different amounts of storage space.
questions.explanation: The chapter states that different types of files require different amounts of storage space.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: Which typically requires MORE storage space: photos or text files?
options: They always need exactly the same space
questions.explanation: The chapter notes that photos typically require more storage space than text files.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: A student says, 'All files take up the same amount of storage no matter what they contain.' Why is this incorrect?
options: Because different types of files, like photos versus text, require different amounts of storage space
Because all files are actually free and take no storage
Because storage rules don't apply to files at all
Because only videos ever use storage space
questions.explanation: The chapter explains that different file types need different amounts of space - for example, photos typically need more space than text files.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: Select ALL of these that are examples of PERMANENT storage.
questions.explanation: Hard drives, USB drives, and cloud storage are permanent storage. RAM is temporary, not permanent.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: Select ALL of these that are examples of TEMPORARY storage.
questions.explanation: RAM is temporary storage. Hard drives, USB drives, and cloud storage are all permanent storage.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: Which comes first in the storage unit sequence: Kilobyte or Megabyte?
questions.explanation: In the storage unit sequence, Kilobyte comes before Megabyte (Bit, Byte, Kilobyte, Megabyte...).

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: A Terabyte (TB) is smaller than a Gigabyte (GB).
questions.explanation: A Terabyte is much larger than a Gigabyte - 1 Terabyte equals 1024 Gigabytes.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: Which of these correctly ranks storage units from LARGEST to SMALLEST?
questions.explanation: From largest to smallest, the correct order is Terabyte, Gigabyte, Megabyte, Kilobyte - the opposite of the usual smallest-to-largest order.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: Which of these is temporary and is cleared when the computer is turned off?
questions.explanation: RAM is temporary storage and is cleared when the computer is turned off.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: Which of these retains its data even when the computer is off?
questions.explanation: ROM retains its data even when the computer is turned off, unlike RAM.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: Why do computers need BOTH permanent and temporary storage, rather than just one type?
options: Because permanent storage saves files long-term while temporary storage (RAM) allows quick, active work - each serves a different purpose
Because temporary storage is completely useless
Because using permanent storage alone is against the rules
Because computers only ever need permanent storage
questions.explanation: Permanent storage keeps files safe long-term, while temporary storage (RAM) supports quick, active tasks - the two work together for different needs.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: Which best summarises the overall difference between storage (like a hard drive) and memory (like RAM)?
options: Storage holds data long-term (like a bookshelf); RAM holds data only while actively working (like a desk)
Storage and RAM are exactly the same thing
Storage is always faster than RAM
questions.explanation: Storage is for long-term keeping, like a bookshelf, while RAM is for active work, like a desk that is cleared once you're done.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: Select ALL of the following that are TRUE about the chapter's overall lessons on storage and memory.
options: Different storage devices suit different needs
Storage capacity and RAM affect a computer differently
Old storage technologies evolved over time into newer ones
Storage capacity is the ONLY thing that affects computer speed
questions.explanation: The chapter teaches that different devices suit different needs, storage and RAM affect computers differently, and storage technology evolved over time. It does NOT say storage capacity alone determines speed - RAM matters more for speed.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: According to the chapter, what should you do to help reduce e-waste and environmental impact from storage devices?
options: Recycle old devices and choose energy-efficient options like SSDs
Buy a new device every week
Avoid using any storage device at all
questions.explanation: The chapter recommends recycling old devices and choosing eco-friendly options like energy-efficient SSDs.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: Which of these best reflects the chapter's 'Golden Rule' about choosing storage types?
options: Important files need permanent storage; quick tasks need temporary storage
Everything should always go in RAM
ROM should be used to store your photos
questions.explanation: The Golden Rule states that important files need permanent storage, while quick tasks need temporary storage.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: Bits are the smallest unit of computer storage.
questions.explanation: The chapter states clearly that bits are the smallest unit of computer storage.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: How are RAM and ROM similar, according to the chapter?
options: Both are described as types of primary/main memory in a computer
Both lose their data when the computer is off
Both are used mainly to store movies
Both work at exactly the same speed
questions.explanation: RAM and ROM are both types of primary or main memory in a computer, even though they behave differently in other ways.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: Which memory type would you check to find the instructions used to start up (boot) the computer?
questions.explanation: ROM contains the instructions that help the computer start up (boot) and connect its devices.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: Which of these best fits the golden rule 'important files need permanent storage'?
options: Saving a family photo to a hard drive
Running a program actively in RAM
questions.explanation: Saving an important family photo to a hard drive is a good example of using permanent storage for something you want to keep long-term.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: Which of these best fits the idea 'quick tasks need temporary storage'?
options: Actively editing a document that hasn't been saved yet, held in RAM
Storing a movie forever on a hard drive
Backing up files to the cloud
Burning a DVD to keep permanently
questions.explanation: An unsaved document being actively edited is held in RAM (temporary storage), which is meant for quick, in-progress tasks.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: What is the overall topic of this chapter?
questions.explanation: The chapter's overall topic is computer storage and memory devices.

questions.topic: Microprocessors, File Sizes and Chapter Review
questions.question: According to the chapter, choosing the right type of storage device depends on factors like speed, capacity, portability, and whether internet access is available.
questions.explanation: Across the chapter, different storage devices are compared by speed (RAM vs ROM, HDD vs SSD), capacity, portability (USB, MicroSD), and internet dependence (cloud vs physical storage).
